meta.title: Who really said "For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Aristotle — Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (1155a). But the famous English wording is W. D. Ross’s 1925 Oxford translation, not Aristotle’s own words.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Aristotle: Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII, ch. 1 (1155a). The quotable English sentence is W. D. Ross's 1925 translation. Greek original and rivals compared.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the real opening move of Book VIII of the Nicomachean Ethics (Bekker 1155a), where Aristotle turns from virtue to friendship. The exact English you see quoted is W. D. Ross’s 1925 Oxford translation — the thought and the argument are Aristotle’s Greek, but these particular English words are Ross’s.

source.heading: Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII, chapter 1

docMeta.dd: W. D. Ross, in The Works of Aristotle Translated into English, vol. IX (Oxford University Press, 1925)

source.excerpt: After what we have said, a discussion of friendship would naturally follow, since it is a virtue or implies virtue, and is besides most necessary with a view to living. For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods; even rich men and those in possession of office and of dominating power are thought to need friends most of all; for what is the use of such prosperity without the opportunity of beneficence, which is exercised chiefly and in its most laudable form towards friends?
trail: The Greek. The line sits at Bekker 1155a in Book 8, chapter 1: “ἄνευ γὰρ φίλων οὐδεὶς ἕλοιτ᾽ ἂν ζῆν, ἔχων τὰ λοιπὰ ἀγαθὰ πάντα” — set out alongside a run of English renderings at WIST Quotations ↗.

The English everyone quotes. W. D. Ross’s translation reads “For without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods” — word for word the popular version, as carried on Wikisource ↗ and in the Internet Classics Archive ↗, which credits its text to Ross.
Listed as sourced. Wikiquote carries the line in its Nicomachean Ethics Book VIII section, cited to 1155a — not among its Misattributed or Disputed entries: Wikiquote: Aristotle ↗.

Other translators, other words. H. Rackham’s Loeb version (Harvard University Press, 1934) renders the same Greek as “no one would choose to live without friends, but possessing all other good things” — see Perseus Digital Library ↗.
source.excerptNote: The famous line is not a standalone aphorism — it is the second sentence of an argument, and Aristotle immediately presses it hardest against the people who look least likely to need friends: the rich and the powerful. Text as given in the Ross translation on Wikisource ↗.

source.reuseChipLabel: Free to reuse in the US
source.useLine: Free to use in the US, including commercially — the Ross translation is US public domain (published 1925). Outside the US, Ross’s English may still be in copyright (he died in 1971); the Greek original is free everywhere.
source.rightsNote: The Greek original has been out of copyright for millennia, but rights here turn on the translation. This exact English wording is W. D. Ross’s, first published in 1925 in volume IX of The Works of Aristotle Translated into English (Oxford University Press) — before 1 January 1931, so it is public domain in the United States, as Wikisource states explicitly ↗. That status does not extend to later renderings: Rackham’s 1934 Loeb and modern translations are separate, later works.

author.name: Aristotle
author.heading: Who was Aristotle?
author.metaLine: 384–322 BC · Greek philosopher, founder of the Lyceum
author.bio: Aristotle studied for two decades under Plato in Athens, tutored the young Alexander the Great, and then founded his own school, the Lyceum. His surviving works — largely lecture material rather than polished books — range across logic, physics, biology, poetics, politics and ethics, and shaped European and Islamic thought for the better part of two thousand years. The Nicomachean Ethics, named for the Nicomachus in Aristotle’s family — usually taken to be his son — is his central account of how a human life goes well, and it gives more room to friendship than to almost any single virtue.

misattribution.heading: The wording is a translator’s, not Aristotle’s
misattribution.intro: Nobody stole this one — the attribution to Aristotle is correct. What gets quietly dropped is that Aristotle wrote in Greek, and the sentence that circulates as his is one particular Englishman’s 1925 phrasing.

items.why: Every aggregator prints this sentence under Aristotle’s name with no translator credit. The words are Ross’s, published in volume IX of The Works of Aristotle Translated into English — Oxford University Press, 1925 ↗.

items.who: H. Rackham, D. P. Chase and others
items.why: The same Greek supports very different English. Rackham’s Loeb (1934) has “no one would choose to live without friends, but possessing all other good things” (Perseus ↗); D. P. Chase’s 1847 version runs “no one would choose to live without friends though he should have all the other good things in the world” (translation comparison at WIST ↗). A version that does not match Ross is not wrong — it is a different translator.

The line is usually printed without its opening “For”, severing it from the sentence it answers, and always without the clause that follows — Aristotle’s point that the rich and powerful need friends most. The full passage is on Wikisource ↗.

The other famous Aristotle-on-friendship line — “a friend is one soul abiding in two bodies” — is a different case entirely: it survives only in Diogenes Laërtius’ Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (p. 188 in the Yonge translation, where Wikiquote ↗ files it), a compilation written some five centuries after Aristotle — not in any surviving work of Aristotle’s own.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Aristotle’s, and it is exactly where people say it is — Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII, chapter 1 (1155a). The sentence, in the form the internet loves, is W. D. Ross’s 1925 English ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Aristotle had just spent seven books building an argument about virtue and the good life. Then he does something odd for a moral philosopher: he devotes two entire books — roughly a fifth of the Nicomachean Ethics — to friendship. This sentence is the hinge, and it is deliberately extreme. Not “friends make life better,” but that a life containing every other good and no friends is one nobody would pick.

The clever part is who he aims at next. The obvious objection is that the rich and powerful can buy company and hardly need friends; Aristotle turns that straight around, arguing they need friends most of all, because what else is prosperity for? That move is what keeps the line from being a greetings-card sentiment.
detailsBody: Aristotle goes on in Book VIII to divide friendship into three kinds — based on utility, on pleasure, and on virtue — and argues that only the third is friendship in the full sense, because it survives once the usefulness and the pleasure run out.

For the record, this is one Aristotle line you can quote safely. He is among the internet’s most abused names, and much of what circulates under it is later paraphrase or second-hand report. This one is in the text, at a citable Bekker number.
context.pull: Not “friends make life better” — that no one would choose the life at all.
